Question: History (git and github basics)
Answer: every change is recorded, so you can see what changed, when, and by whom.

Question: Collaboration (git and github basics)
Answer: many people can work on the same project at once without overwriting each other.

Question: Recovery (git and github basics)
Answer: you can undo a bad change or restore a deleted file from history.

Question: Parallel work (git and github basics)
Answer: branches let you build a feature in isolation and merge it when it is ready.

Question: Accountability and audit (git and github basics)
Answer: each change carries an author and a message that explains intent.

Question: Git (git and github basics)
Answer: a free, open source, distributed version control system that runs locally.

Question: GitHub (git and github basics)
Answer: a cloud platform that hosts Git repositories and adds collaboration, automation and security features.

Question: Repository (git and github basics)
Answer: a project's files plus the complete history of changes to them.

Question: Commit (git and github basics)
Answer: a snapshot of changes with a unique SHA, author, timestamp and message.

Question: Branch (git and github basics)
Answer: a lightweight movable pointer to a commit, used to isolate work.

Question: HEAD (git and github basics)
Answer: a pointer to the branch or commit you currently have checked out.

Question: Remote (git and github basics)
Answer: a copy of the repository hosted elsewhere, conventionally named origin.

Question: Default branch (git and github basics)
Answer: the branch GitHub shows first and targets for pull requests, usually main.

Question: Personal account (git and github basics)
Answer: an individual identity on GitHub; every user has exactly one to sign in with.

Question: Organization (git and github basics)
Answer: a shared account that owns repositories and grants access to members through roles and teams.

Question: Enterprise account (git and github basics)
Answer: an account that centrally manages policies, billing and identity for multiple organizations.

Question: @mentions (git and github basics)
Answer: @username or @org/team notifies that person or team.

Question: Issue and PR references (git and github basics)
Answer: #123 links to issue or pull request 123 in the same repository; owner/repo#123 links across repositories.

Question: Commit references (git and github basics)
Answer: pasting a commit SHA turns it into a link.

Question: Task lists (git and github basics)
Answer: checkboxes that show progress in the issue list.

Question: Alerts (git and github basics)
Answer: > [!NOTE], > [!TIP], > [!IMPORTANT], > [!WARNING] and > [!CAUTION] render as coloured callouts.

Question: Diagrams and maths (git and github basics)
Answer: Mermaid code blocks render as diagrams, and $...$ renders LaTeX maths.

Question: Emoji shortcodes (git and github basics)
Answer: tada: style codes.

Question: README (repositories)
Answer: the rendered front page of a repository explaining what it is and how to use it.

Question: LICENSE (repositories)
Answer: a file granting legal permission to use, modify and share the code; without it, all rights are reserved.

Question: CONTRIBUTING (repositories)
Answer: guidelines that GitHub links when someone opens an issue or pull request.

Question: CODEOWNERS (repositories)
Answer: a file mapping paths to owners who are automatically requested for review.

Question: SECURITY.md (repositories)
Answer: the security policy describing how to report vulnerabilities privately.

Question: Community health files (repositories)
Answer: the standard set of files (code of conduct, contributing, security, support) that can be defaulted from an organization's .github repository.

Question: Pulse (repositories)
Answer: the Insights summary of recent pull request and issue activity.

Question: Traffic (repositories)
Answer: the Insights view of views, clones and referrers over the last 14 days, for people with push access.

Question: Dependency graph (repositories)
Answer: the list of packages a repository depends on and that depend on it, built from manifest files.

Question: Dependency insights (repositories)
Answer: an organization-wide view of dependencies, vulnerabilities and licenses across repositories.

Question: Star (repositories)
Answer: a bookmark and a public signal of appreciation; not a notification subscription.

Question: Feature preview (repositories)
Answer: a user setting to opt in to early versions of new GitHub features.

Question: Issue (collaboration)
Answer: a tracked unit of work such as a bug, feature or task.

Question: Pull request (collaboration)
Answer: a proposal to merge changes from a head branch into a base branch, with review and checks.

Question: Draft pull request (collaboration)
Answer: a pull request marked not ready; it cannot be merged until marked ready for review.

Question: Discussion (collaboration)
Answer: a forum-style thread for questions, ideas and announcements that is not a unit of work.

Question: Sub-issue (collaboration)
Answer: an issue nested under a parent issue to break down larger work.

Question: Watching (collaboration)
Answer: subscribing to a repository's activity at a chosen level; different from starring.

Question: Participating (collaboration)
Answer: being involved in a thread by authoring, commenting, being assigned, mentioned or requested for review.

Question: Custom watch (collaboration)
Answer: a watch level that adds chosen event types such as releases on top of participating notifications.

Question: Notification inbox (collaboration)
Answer: the web view of notifications with Done, Save and custom filters.

Question: Gist (collaboration)
Answer: a small Git repository for sharing snippets, either public or secret (unlisted).

Question: Wiki (collaboration)
Answer: repository documentation pages stored in a separate Git repository.

Question: GitHub Pages (collaboration)
Answer: static website hosting from a repository branch, folder or Actions workflow.

Question: Workflow (modern development)
Answer: an automated process defined in a YAML file in .github/workflows/.

Question: Event (modern development)
Answer: the trigger that starts a workflow, such as push, pull_request, schedule or workflow_dispatch.

Question: Job (modern development)
Answer: a set of steps that run on the same runner; jobs run in parallel unless one needs another.

Question: Step (modern development)
Answer: a single task in a job: a shell command (run) or a reusable action (uses).

Question: Action (modern development)
Answer: a reusable unit of automation, often from GitHub Marketplace, such as actions/checkout.

Question: Runner (modern development)
Answer: the machine that executes a job; GitHub-hosted (managed Linux, Windows or macOS) or self-hosted.

Question: Inline suggestions (modern development)
Answer: code completions as you type, from a single line to a whole function, plus next edit suggestions.

Question: Copilot Chat (modern development)
Answer: ask questions in the IDE, on GitHub.com or in GitHub Mobile: explain this code, write a test, why is this failing.

Question: Agent mode (modern development)
Answer: an IDE mode where Copilot plans and carries out a multi-step task on its own.

Question: Copilot cloud agent (modern development)
Answer: an agent that works on GitHub itself, in the background, and hands back a branch or pull request. The GH-900 outline calls this the coding agent, its earlier name.

Question: Copilot code review (modern development)
Answer: Copilot reviews a pull request and leaves comments with suggested fixes.

Question: Multi-model choice (modern development)
Answer: pick which AI model answers in Chat and agent mode.

Question: Policy management (modern development)
Answer: admins decide which features are on (Chat, agent mode, the cloud agent, Copilot CLI), which models are allowed, and whether suggestions matching public code are blocked.

Question: Content exclusion (modern development)
Answer: admins can stop Copilot using specific files or repositories as context.

Question: Audit logs (modern development)
Answer: Copilot events appear in the organization or enterprise audit log.

Question: IP indemnity (modern development)
Answer: under GitHub's product terms, organization plans include legal protection if Copilot output is claimed to infringe copyright, subject to conditions such as the public code filter.

Question: Data handling (modern development)
Answer: by default, Business and Enterprise prompts and code are not used to train models.

Question: Shared organization knowledge (modern development)
Answer: the outline mentions Enterprise knowledge bases (curated documentation Copilot can draw on). In current GitHub Docs that role is filled by Copilot Spaces, which collect code, docs and notes as context and can be shared across a team.

Question: Codespace (modern development)
Answer: a cloud-hosted development environment on a GitHub-managed virtual machine, opened in the browser or an IDE.

Question: devcontainer.json (modern development)
Answer: the dev container configuration that defines a codespace's image, tools, extensions and setup commands.

Question: Prebuild (modern development)
Answer: a prepared codespace image that makes large repositories start faster.

Question: Text (project management)
Answer: free text, such as a short note.

Question: Number (project management)
Answer: numeric values such as story points or estimates.

Question: Date (project management)
Answer: a single date, such as a target date for roadmap bars.

Question: Single select (project management)
Answer: one value from a list you define, such as Status, Priority or Team.

Question: Iteration (project management)
Answer: repeating time boxes (sprints) with a start date and length, with breaks if needed.

Question: View (project management)
Answer: a saved layout plus filter, sort, grouping and visible fields in a project.

Question: Custom field (project management)
Answer: project-level metadata (text, number, date, single select or iteration) added to every item.

Question: Iteration field (project management)
Answer: a field of repeating time boxes such as two-week sprints.

Question: Draft issue (project management)
Answer: a project item that exists only in the project until converted into a repository issue.

Question: Item closed (project management)
Answer: set Status to Done when an issue is closed.

Question: Pull request merged (project management)
Answer: set Status to Done when a linked PR merges.

Question: Item added to project (project management)
Answer: set a starting Status such as Todo.

Question: Item reopened (project management)
Answer: move the item back to an active status.

Question: Auto-add to project (project management)
Answer: automatically add new issues or PRs from a repository that match a filter (for example is:issue label:bug).

Question: Auto-archive items (project management)
Answer: archive items that match a filter, such as closed more than two weeks ago, to keep views tidy.

Question: Label (project management)
Answer: a coloured tag for categorizing issues, pull requests and discussions; many per item.

Question: Milestone (project management)
Answer: a repository-level goal with an optional due date and a progress bar; one per item.

Question: Assignee (project management)
Answer: a person responsible for an issue or pull request; up to 10 per item.

Question: Saved reply (project management)
Answer: a personal reusable comment snippet inserted when responding to issues and pull requests.

Question: Two-factor authentication (2FA) (privacy security administration)
Answer: signing in with a password plus a second factor such as an app code, security key, passkey or GitHub Mobile.

Question: Passkey (privacy security administration)
Answer: a phishing-resistant WebAuthn credential usable as a second factor or for passwordless sign-in.

Question: Recovery codes (privacy security administration)
Answer: one-time codes that restore access if you lose your 2FA device.

Question: Fine-grained personal access token (privacy security administration)
Answer: a token limited to chosen repositories and permissions, with an expiry.

Question: Least privilege (privacy security administration)
Answer: granting the minimum access a person needs.

Question: Triage role (privacy security administration)
Answer: manages issues and pull requests without write access to code.

Question: Maintain role (privacy security administration)
Answer: manages a repository without sensitive or destructive settings.

Question: Security manager (privacy security administration)
Answer: organization role that manages security alerts and settings across all repositories.

Question: Outside collaborator (privacy security administration)
Answer: a non-member given access to specific organization repositories.

Question: Base permissions (privacy security administration)
Answer: the default repository role every organization member receives.

Question: Team (privacy security administration)
Answer: a group of organization members granted repository access together; can be nested.

Question: Layering (privacy security administration)
Answer: many rulesets can apply to the same branch at once. Their rules combine, and the most restrictive wins.

Question: Enforcement status (privacy security administration)
Answer: a ruleset can be Active or Disabled, and on Enterprise it can run in Evaluate mode to report what would be blocked without blocking it.

Question: Bypass list (privacy security administration)
Answer: named roles, teams or apps can be allowed to bypass, which is explicit and auditable.

Question: Organization scope (privacy security administration)
Answer: organizations on GitHub Enterprise can define rulesets once at the organization level and target many repositories by name pattern or property.

Question: Tags and pushes (privacy security administration)
Answer: rulesets can protect tags, and push rulesets can block pushes to private or internal repositories by file path, size or extension.

Question: Availability (privacy security administration)
Answer: rulesets work on public repositories on every plan, and on private repositories with GitHub Pro, Team or Enterprise.

Question: Visibility (privacy security administration)
Answer: anyone with read access can see which rulesets apply, which explains why a push was rejected.

Question: Audit log (privacy security administration)
Answer: the record of security-relevant actions taken in an organization or enterprise.

Question: Ruleset (privacy security administration)
Answer: a named, layered set of branch, tag or push rules with an enforcement status and bypass list.

Question: Branch protection rule (privacy security administration)
Answer: a single rule set on a branch name pattern in one repository.

Question: Enterprise Managed Users (privacy security administration)
Answer: accounts created and controlled by the company's identity provider, confined to the enterprise.

Question: Internal visibility (privacy security administration)
Answer: repository visibility for all members of an enterprise, used for InnerSource.

Question: Dependabot alerts (privacy security administration)
Answer: warn when a dependency has a known vulnerability, using the dependency graph and the GitHub Advisory Database.

Question: Dependabot security updates (privacy security administration)
Answer: open pull requests that upgrade a vulnerable dependency to a fixed version.

Question: Dependabot version updates (privacy security administration)
Answer: open pull requests to keep dependencies current, configured in .github/dependabot.yml.

Question: Secret scanning (privacy security administration)
Answer: detects committed credentials such as API keys and tokens.

Question: Push protection (privacy security administration)
Answer: blocks a push that contains a detected secret before it reaches the repository.

Question: Code scanning (privacy security administration)
Answer: static analysis, typically with CodeQL, that finds vulnerabilities and coding errors and shows alerts on pull requests.

Question: Security advisories (privacy security administration)
Answer: let maintainers privately discuss, fix and publish a vulnerability, and request a CVE.

Question: Quality through many eyes (github community)
Answer: more reviewers find more bugs, including security bugs.

Question: Speed (github community)
Answer: you build on existing libraries instead of writing everything yourself.

Question: Shared cost (github community)
Answer: companies that all need the same tool can maintain it together.

Question: Learning and career (github community)
Answer: contributions are public evidence of skill, and reading real code is how many people learn.

Question: Transparency and trust (github community)
Answer: you can inspect exactly what the software does.

Question: Avoiding lock-in (github community)
Answer: if a vendor disappears, the code is still there.

Question: Free features for public repositories (github community)
Answer: unlimited public repositories, free Actions minutes on standard GitHub-hosted runners, and security features such as Dependabot alerts, secret scanning and code scanning at no cost.

Question: GitHub Sponsors (github community)
Answer: direct funding for maintainers (see below).

Question: Community health tooling (github community)
Answer: templates, community standards checklist, Discussions and moderation tools.

Question: Security help (github community)
Answer: the GitHub Advisory Database, private vulnerability reporting and security advisories with CVE requests.

Question: Programmes (github community)
Answer: for example GitHub Stars (recognising community leaders), GitHub Education for students and teachers, and the GitHub Archive Program, which preserves public code for the long term.

Question: FUNDING.yml (github community)
Answer: a file in .github/ that shows a Sponsor button linking to funding platforms.

Question: GitHub Stars (github community)
Answer: GitHub's recognition programme for influential community members; unrelated to starring a repository.

Question: Apps (github community)
Answer: integrations installed on an account or organization, such as CI services, code quality tools, project management bridges or chat notifications. Some are free, some paid, billed through GitHub.

Question: Actions (github community)
Answer: reusable building blocks for GitHub Actions workflows, referenced with uses:.

Question: Open source (github community)
Answer: software whose code is published under a license allowing use, study, change and redistribution.

Question: Permissive license (github community)
Answer: a license such as MIT or Apache 2.0 that allows reuse in closed-source products.

Question: Copyleft license (github community)
Answer: a license such as GPL that requires distributed derivatives to use the same license.

Question: InnerSource (github community)
Answer: applying open source practices to code shared inside one company.

Question: Topic (github community)
Answer: a tag on a public repository that makes it discoverable on topic pages and in search.

Question: GitHub Marketplace (github community)
Answer: the catalogue of apps and actions that extend GitHub.
